newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine drug case said linked to mafia.
newsitem.headline: Argentine drug case said linked to mafia.

text.p: The judge who indicted Argentina's soccer star Diego Maradona's manager, Guillermo Coppola, said on Saturday he believed the drug smuggling ring he is investigating has connections with the Italian mafia.

"The Coppola case has very important connections with the Italian mafia," Judge Hernan Bernasconi said in an interview with daily La Nacion. "But I will announce each ramification that it might have, as I obtain proof of the participation of the individuals that are involved in this network."

This new development in a case that has gripped Argentina's attention for two weeks came after the testimony "of a man who spoke of the link between Guillermo Coppola with the Italian mafia," Bernasconi said.
Bernasconi will follow up his investigation in a meeting in coming days with an Italian public prosecutor who was to arrive in Buenos Aires late on Saturday.

Sandro Ausiello, a public prosecutor from Turin in Italy, was following another case involving an alleged transfer of $12 million from a bank account in Uruguay's capital Montevideo to Holland said to be part of deal involving an 11-ton drug shipment to Europe.
Bernasconi and Ausiello will meet to see if there are any connections between the two cases.

Coppola was arrested two weeks ago after a pound (500 grams) of cocaine was found in his luxury appartment during a police raid. He was charged on Thursday with possession of drugs for sale and could face up to 20 years in prison.
The silver-haired, bronzed 49-year-old said the drugs were planted.

Maradona's brother-in-law, Gabriel Esposito, ex-soccer player Alberto Tarantini and his girlfriend were also arrested but were only being sentenced to drug rehabilitation. Three other men arrested with Coppola were indicted.

Maradona was said to be distraught at Coppola's arrest and threatened this week to uncover "hidden and dark political and economic interests" behind his friend's prosecution. But the hero of Argentina's 1986 World Cup title backed down on Thursday, expressing through his attorneys his "trust in the justice system and especially Judge Hernan Bernasconi."
